nationality_or_literary_tradition: African-American; the investigative pamphlet and the literature of anti-lynching
literary_identity: Journalist, editor and activist; the founder of the modern investigative journalism of racial terror and the central figure of the anti-lynching movement.
biography: Born Ida Bell Wells in Holly Springs, Mississippi, on 16 July 1862, six months before emancipation; she was orphaned at sixteen and supported her siblings as a teacher, then moved to Memphis and edited the Free Speech and Headlight. After the lynching of three friends in 1892 she published Southern Horrors (1892) and was driven from Memphis; she toured Britain and the United States, married the lawyer Ferdinand Barnett in 1895, and was a founder of the NAACP in 1909. She died in Chicago on 25 March 1931.
literary_profile: Wells invented the modern documentary pamphlet: her anti-lynching reports collect statistics, court records, newspaper accounts and her own interviews, and they destroy the myth of the black rapist with evidence while naming the economic motive behind the terror. Her prose is controlled, factual and utterly fearless, and The Red Record is the founding text of American investigative journalism on race.
stylistic_characteristics: Documented statistics; case by case narrative; the exposure of newspaper lies; direct indictment of named officials; irony and controlled anger; the pamphlet and the lecture as political instruments.
intellectual_concerns: Lynching and racial terror; the sexual politics of the myth of the black rapist; the economic competition behind the violence; the failure of the law and the churches; the black woman's testimony; the American South and the nation's silence.
historical_significance: Wells is the founding figure of anti-lynching journalism and one of the most important American writers of non-fiction: Southern Horrors and The Red Record created the documentary literature of racial terror, and her work is the direct ancestor of the civil rights journalism of the twentieth century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the local-colour story of the mining camps
literary_identity: Poet and short-story writer; the inventor of the American western story and the founder of the local-colour movement.
biography: Born in Albany, New York, on 25 August 1836; the family moved to California in 1854, and he worked as a miner, a teacher, a journalist and an editor of the Overland Monthly, in which 'The Luck of Roaring Camp' (1868) made him famous. He was professor of literature at Berkeley in 1871 and then lived in New York and Europe, serving as American consul at Crefeld and Glasgow. He died at Camberley, England, on 5 May 1902.
literary_profile: Harte invented the American western story: his mining-camp tales of California — the gambler, the dance-hall girl, the Chinese cook, the runaway — fixed the characters and the sentiment that would dominate the American imagination of the West. He was also the first editor to pay serious attention to regional writing, and the Overland Monthly under his editorship launched the local-colour movement that Twain, Jewett and Freeman would develop.
stylistic_characteristics: The single dramatic scene with a surprise ending; sentiment about the outcast and the child; dialect and stock characters; precise description of the mining camp; verse with a strong narrative line.
intellectual_concerns: The California gold rush and the mining camp; the outcast, the gambler and the prostitute; the American West and its myth; the racial and ethnic margins of the frontier; death and sentiment; the clash of civilisation and wilderness.
historical_significance: Harte is the founder of the American western story and of the local-colour movement: 'The Luck of Roaring Camp', 'The Outcasts of Poker Flat' and 'Tennessee's Partner' are the founding texts of the American literature of the West, and his Overland Monthly created the market for regional writing in America.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the dialect tale and the framing of black oral narrative
literary_identity: Journalist and writer; the author of the Uncle Remus stories, the most influential collection of African-American folklore in the nineteenth century.
biography: Born in Eatonton, Georgia, on 9 December 1848, the illegitimate son of an Irish day labourer; at thirteen he was apprenticed to a plantation newspaper, the Countryman, where he lived on the Turnwold plantation and heard the African-American animal tales from the enslaved workers. He worked for the Savannah Morning News and from 1876 for the Atlanta Constitution, where the Uncle Remus sketches appeared from 1878. Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings was published in 1880. He died in Atlanta on 3 July 1908.
literary_profile: Harris wrote the American dialect tale as a record of black oral narrative: the Brer Rabbit stories are African-American folk tales collected with real fidelity, and their trickster hero is one of the great creations of American literature. The frame of the kindly old freedman telling stories to a white boy is also a myth of the plantation that later black writers — Chesnutt above all — had to dismantle, and Harris's work must be read in both lights.
stylistic_characteristics: Frame narrative in which the tale is told to a listener; phonetic dialect transcription of great care; the trickster plot of the weaker against the stronger; the comic ending; the plantation setting and its idealisation.
intellectual_concerns: African-American folklore and oral tradition; the trickster and the powerless; the plantation myth and its ideology; childhood and storytelling; the post-Reconstruction South; the relation of black and white Southerners.
historical_significance: Harris collected and preserved the most important body of African-American folklore of the nineteenth century and introduced Brer Rabbit to the world: his dialect transcription is a landmark of American dialect writing, and the Uncle Remus books are central — and contested — documents of American race and literature.
major_influences: The enslaved storytellers of the Turnwold plantation

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Pre-Raphaelite lyric, the verse drama and the criticism
literary_identity: Poet, dramatist and critic; the greatest technical virtuoso of Victorian poetry and the most scandalous poet of the 1860s.
biography: Born in London on 5 April 1837 and brought up on the Isle of Wight and in Northumberland; he was educated at Eton and Balliol College, Oxford, where he met Dante Gabriel Rossetti and William Morris and left without a degree in 1860. Atalanta in Calydon (1865) and Poems and Ballads (1866) made him famous and notorious; he lived with the painter Simeon Solomon's circle and with the adventurer Richard Burton's, drank heavily, and in 1879 was taken in by his friend Theodore Watts-Dunton at Putney, where he lived quietly until his death on 10 April 1909.
literary_profile: Swinburne wrote the most musical English verse of the century: his great subject is the conflict of pleasure and pain, of paganism and Christianity, and his method is the incantation of sound — anapaestic rhythms, alliteration, refrain and repetition pushed to the point where the verse becomes almost pure music. He was also a considerable dramatic poet, a great critic of Elizabethan drama, and a political republican whose songs on Italy and Ireland gave Victorian radicalism its poetry.
stylistic_characteristics: Incantatory anapaestic and trochaic metres; heavy alliteration and assonance; refrain and repetition; a vocabulary of sea, flame, blood and flowers; the sado-masochistic image; rhetorical denunciation; the classical choric ode.
intellectual_concerns: Love, pain and the death of the beloved; paganism against Christianity; liberty, republicanism and the Italian risorgimento; the sea and the elements; the body and its pleasures; childhood and memory.
historical_significance: Swinburne is the greatest technical poet of the Victorian age and the central figure of the English Decadence: Poems and Ballads changed the possibilities of English verse, his influence on the 1890s, on Hardy's poetry and on the modern lyric is enormous, and his criticism of the Elizabethan dramatists remains standard reading.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the narrative poem, the socialist romance and the literature of design
literary_identity: Poet, designer, translator and socialist; the author of The Earthly Paradise and News from Nowhere, and the most complete artist of the Victorian age.
biography: Born at Walthamstow on 24 March 1834, the son of a financier; he was educated at Marlborough and Exeter College, Oxford, where he met Edward Burne-Jones and was drawn to the Pre-Raphaelites. He founded the firm of Morris, Marshall, Faulkner and Co in 1861, masterminded the Kelmscott Press in 1891, and wrote The Defence of Guenevere (1858), The Life and Death of Jason (1867), The Earthly Paradise (1868-70), Sigurd the Volsung (1876) and News from Nowhere (1890). He was a founder of the Socialist League in 1884 and died at Hammersmith on 3 October 1896.
literary_profile: Morris wrote the great narrative poetry of the Victorian age: his subject is the heroic and the mythic past, and his method is the long, fluent, objective narrative in which the story carries the emotion. He was also the first English writer to make the utopian romance a serious political form, and his work on design, printing and the decorative arts made him the central figure of the English arts and crafts movement.
stylistic_characteristics: Long, even, unrhymed or heroic-couplet narrative; the archaic and the Norse-Teutonic vocabulary; the objective storytelling with little psychological commentary; the catalogue of the decorative and the natural; the dream-vision frame.
intellectual_concerns: The heroic past and the death of the hero; love and fate; the Norse and classical myths; labour, craft and the dignity of work; socialism and the utopian future; the natural world and the decorative art.
historical_significance: Morris is the central figure of the English arts and crafts movement and one of the great narrative poets of the century: The Earthly Paradise and Sigurd the Volsung restored the long poem to English literature, News from Nowhere is the classic English socialist utopia, and his designs, printing and prose romances shaped the modern book and the modern fantasy.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the symbolist lyric, the criticism of decadence and the essay on the dance
literary_identity: Poet, critic and editor; the central impresario of the English Decadence and the first English critic of the Symbolist movement.
biography: Born at Milford Haven on 28 February 1865; he was brought up in Devon and London, edited the Savoy with Aubrey Beardsley in 1896, and published Days and Nights (1889), London Nights (1895) and The Symbolist Movement in Literature (1899), the book through which Yeats, Eliot and Pound learned about French poetry. He edited the seven-volume Collected Works of Dowson and the plays of Webster. A mental breakdown in 1908 ended his central period; he lived on in Cornwall and Kent and died at Wittersham on 22 January 1945.
literary_profile: Symons wrote the poetry of urban night and the prose of aesthetic criticism: his lyrics of the music hall, the ballet and the prostitute's room made the city a place of the senses, and his Symbolist book changed the course of English and American poetry by teaching a generation that literature is the expression of an invisible world through symbol. His criticism of the dance, of Beardsley, of Huysmans and of Wagner is the central body of English Decadent prose.
stylistic_characteristics: The short lyric built on a single mood; the city at night; the dance rhythms of the music hall; musical repetition and refrain; the prose essay of aesthetic appreciation; the critical definition by evocation.
intellectual_concerns: The city and its pleasures; the dancer and the music hall; the prostitute and the outsider; sexual desire and its costs; the Symbolist theory of art; the relation of the arts; decadence and exhaustion.
historical_significance: Symons is the central English critic of the Decadence and the man who introduced Symbolism to the English-speaking world: The Symbolist Movement in Literature is one of the most influential critical books ever published in English, and his poetry and his Savoy editorship made him the impresario of the 1890s.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Decadent lyric and the short story of exhaustion
literary_identity: Poet and short-story writer; the most pure and the most tragic of the English Decadent poets.
biography: Born at Lee, Kent, on 2 August 1867; he was educated at Queen's College, Oxford, but left without a degree, and worked in his father's failing dock business. He fell in love with the eleven-year-old daughter of the proprietor of a London Italian restaurant, and the hopeless passion of his life, together with the deaths of his parents and his own alcoholism, produced the verse of Verses (1896) and Decorations (1899). He died of tuberculosis at Catford on 23 February 1900, at thirty-two.
literary_profile: Dowson wrote the poetry of renunciation and exhaustion: his lyrics are short, perfectly made and obsessive, and their subject is the love that cannot be possessed, the wine that cannot console and the faith that has been lost. His prose, especially the stories collected in Dilemmas (1895) and the unfinished novel Madame de Vionnet, is the finest Decadent prose after Pater, and his influence on the modern lyric is out of all proportion to the smallness of his output.
stylistic_characteristics: Short lyric metres of great smoothness; refrain and repetition; the Latin refrain ('non sum qualis eram bonae sub regno Cynarae'); the exhausted cadence; imagery of wine, roses, twilight and the sea.
intellectual_concerns: Hopeless love and renunciation; the loss of faith; wine and exhaustion; the passing of youth; the city at evening; the memory of a happiness that never was.
historical_significance: Dowson is the purest of the English Decadent poets and the author of some of the most quoted lines in the language: 'Non sum qualis eram bonae sub regno Cynarae' and 'They are not long, the weeping and the laughter' are permanent parts of English poetry, and his small body of work has influenced Yeats, Eliot and the modern lyric of loss.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Catholic lyric, the critical essay and the poetry of the Rhymers' Club
literary_identity: Poet, critic and essayist; the most learned and the most tormented of the English Decadent poets, and a founding member of the Rhymers' Club.
biography: Born at Broadstairs on 15 March 1867, the son of a captain in the Royal Army Medical Corps; he was educated at Winchester and New College, Oxford, where he became a Catholic in 1891 and took a first in classics. He was a founder of the Rhymers' Club with Yeats and Dowson, wrote Poems (1895) and Ireland and Other Poems (1897), and published the finest critical essays of his generation on Hardy, Pater and the Celtic revival. He drank himself to death in London on 4 October 1902.
literary_profile: Johnson wrote the poetry of faith and damnation: a Catholic convert who could not reconcile his religion with his desires, he produced lyrics of great technical finish and terrible interior tension, and his critical prose — collected in Post Liminium and Reviews and Critical Papers — is the most learned criticism of the 1890s. He was the scholar of the Decadence, and his essays on the Celtic literature of Ireland helped to make the Irish revival possible.
stylistic_characteristics: Classical and medieval metres handled with learning; the stanza of Wyatt and the seventeenth century revived; the Catholic imagery of the Mass and the martyrs; the elegiac and penitential tone; the critical essay of close reading.
intellectual_concerns: Catholic faith and sin; the divided self and the impossibility of peace; Ireland and the Celtic past; the English literary tradition; friendship and loneliness; death and the last things.
historical_significance: Johnson is the finest Catholic poet of the English 1890s and one of the best critics of his generation: his essays on Hardy and Pater are standard, his Poems are the most formally accomplished of the Rhymers' Club volumes, and his influence on Yeats's criticism and on the Catholic literary revival was decisive.
